prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated free of Doppler and recoil shifts, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock (Katori and Ye) as my final single-part position, unchanged from round 1. After reading the full exchange I find nobody contests the science: the magic-wavelength lattice lets thousands of atoms be interrogated with no first-order light shift and no Doppler or recoil broadening, and independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) reproduce 1e-18-level performance and agree with each other in direct clock comparisons, including over fibre. That is the independent confirmation I ask of any claimed advance. The chair's question on distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes has a concrete answer in terms of what is awarded: Hall and Hansch gave the comb, the ruler for optical frequencies, and Wineland gave control of one trapped quantum system. The lattice clock is a different object, a many-atom ensemble whose stability and systematics improve together, and it has produced physics of its own, namely millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tight limits on drifting constants and many-body effects in the clock. On credit, Katori made the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock and Ye took it to the accuracy and stability frontier. Two names need no arbitrary cut among the principals, even though others contributed. I support recognition now rather than after the redefinition of the second, because the redefinition is a metrology decision and the scientific achievement already stands.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes: a reader who sees the lattice clock as a refinement of comb-based spectroscopy and ion clocks will see an instrument improvement and not a new door. I think that reading is wrong, but it is a judgment about how much the many-atom magic-wavelength step counts as new, and the citation must say so explicitly. The second reservation is attribution. Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Ovsiannikov and others sit outside the two names, and Olsson and Lindroth are right that I should not dismiss them lightly; the committee's expert review has to verify the dates of Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and 2005 strontium demonstration against the parallel work in Paris and Boulder. Third, Danielsson and Mehlig are right that the clock has so far produced limits on new physics, not detections, and that is a real difference from a discovery of a new phenomenon, although I weigh the new measurement regime as a result in itself.

responses.point: Kroll calls the credit the cleanest on the shortlist but admits the 2005 and 2012 prizes are adjacent ground, and discloses time in John Hall's laboratory and proximity to JILA.
responses.response: I agree that the citation is where this is won or lost, and I accept your wording with one change, which is to name the many-atom, Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation explicitly, since that is what separates the lattice from the comb and from a single ion. I do not think your year in Hall's laboratory requires recusal: you have no co-authorship with Ye or Katori, and the prize would honour the lattice concept and its performance, not the comb. As Chair I would ask that it stay on record and that the committee's reviewers, not you, handle the question of Ye's comb-based work. Your requirement of documentary evidence on roles applies equally to my own IceCube preference, and I accept it.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B045 for its universal bulk invariant but says B022 is the safer prize if a clean, uncontested allocation is weighted above field-level influence, and describes the lattice clock as an application of known atomic physics.
responses.response: I take the second half of your statement seriously and I think it is the right criterion for a final public position. On the first half I respectfully disagree that the clock only applies known physics. Magic-wavelength trapping and Lamb-Dicke confinement were individually known, but that a lattice could hold thousands of atoms with the two clock levels shifted equally, with no first-order shift, and then be driven to 1e-18 was not an obvious outcome, and the many-body effects that appeared were not planned. On B045 I lack the expertise to settle the invariant versus experiment question and I rely on you. I would only say that a second topology prize after 2016 needs the citation to isolate the Z2 and quantum spin Hall discovery, and that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit has to be settled in the documents before I could rank it above the clock.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B022 first but asks whether Katori and Ye are the right two names given Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and Lemonde, and ranks IceCube low because of collaboration scale and thin independent confirmation.
responses.response: I accept your IceCube objection and it is the reason I have moved B046 from my first place to an alternative: the diffuse flux is well established but source identification is thin and no second detector yet confirms it at comparable strength. On the clock, I agree we should not decide the two-name question from memory. My position is that Katori has priority for the proposal and first demonstration and Ye for the performance frontier, and I would support this only if the background review confirms those dates and shows that Lemonde or Hinkley contributed refinements, not the founding step. If the review shows otherwise I would rather say so openly than make a fragile award.

responses.point: Danielsson asks whether a clock tells us a clue from nature rather than a limit, and prefers B002 (BAO) while saying he would not block B022 and that the redefinition belongs to metrology.
responses.response: I appreciate that you separate your own weighting from a committee view and that you would not block B022. On your criterion, my answer is that the lattice clock has already yielded a clue of a kind: it measures gravitational redshift across millimetres and shows many-body behaviour in a clock, which no earlier clock could. I accept that limits on constants and dark matter are still limits. I would apply the same criterion evenly to other measurement-led cases, and it would not by itself exclude BAO, which I regard as a strong future candidate. My difficulty with BAO this year is the credit: two survey collaborations, and the Peebles-Yu and Sunyaev-Zeldovich predictions, make a trio partly arbitrary.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B045 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp but concedes B022 has far broader support and says he would sooner see it awarded cleanly than force a contested trio.
responses.response: Thank you for that frankness. I do not claim expertise on topological insulators and I defer to you and Mehlig on the physics. What makes me hesitate on B045 is the credit structure you describe yourself: BHZ with Zhang deceased, the 3D work of Hasan, Moore, Balents and Fu, and the 2016 prize. I would keep B045 as my first alternative because the science is mature, and if the documentary review resolves Mele versus Hasan and the 2D versus 3D question in a clean way, I would reconsider it for a future year. For this year, your own stated condition for supporting B022 appears to be met.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-system prizes; this depends on citation wording and on a judgment I cannot make for the whole committee.
Priority among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and Takamoto for the proposal, first demonstration and accuracy frontier, which I recall only from memory and which expert review should check.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would change the committee's view; I think it should not, but others disagree.
For B045, whether the committee treats 2D quantum spin Hall and 3D topological insulators as one achievement and how to credit BHZ; I rely on colleagues for this.
statement.conflict_note: No collaboration with Katori, Ye or any credited name for B022, B045 or B046; my own field is astroparticle physics and detector instrumentation (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur). My earlier first-place ranking of B046 and field adjacency to it no longer drive my position, since I now keep it only as an alternative. I note Kroll's disclosure on John Hall and JILA and Johansson's disclosure on B039 and B032, neither of which affects my configuration. As Chair I am responsible for the process and I do not count support totals as a substitute for the scientific judgment recorded here.
